name: Conjunction fallacy
statement: Told about Linda, 85% of 142 undergraduates judged she was more likely to be a feminist bank teller than a bank teller.
meaning: The conjunction rule says the probability of A and B together can never exceed the probability of A alone, because every case of both is a case of each. Tversky and Kahneman argued that people judge probability by resemblance, so an added detail that fits the description can make the narrower statement look likelier than the wider one. They kept two findings apart, and the distinction is easy to lose. When one person compares the conjunction with its constituent and rates the conjunction higher, that is the conjunction fallacy. When separate groups rate one statement each and the group mean for the conjunction comes out higher, that is a conjunction error, which is a claim about averages rather than about any individual.

origin.note: "Extensional Versus Intuitive Reasoning: The Conjunction Fallacy in Probability Judgment" ran the problem across domains, from Linda and Bill to medical prognosis, Wimbledon finals and suspicion of criminal acts. The paper says the first studies of the conjunction rule were conducted in 1974 and that the project tested more than 3,000 subjects.

evidence: Eighty-eight UBC undergraduates first ranked the eight statements for each description by how far Bill and Linda resembled the class. The predicted order came out for 87% of them on Bill and 85% on Linda, which was the expected result. Ranking the same statements by probability produced almost the same pattern. Across three groups, statistically naive students, students with a statistics course and doctoral students in decision science, direct-test violations ran 92%, 86% and 83% for Bill and 89%, 90% and 85% for Linda. The overall rate in direct tests was 88%, and the correlation between mean probability and mean representativeness ranks was .96 for Bill and .98 for Linda. Statistical training made no difference. Tversky and Kahneman then stripped the problem down. Given only the two statements and asked which was more probable, 85% of 142 UBC undergraduates picked the conjunction. Asked to rate both on a nine-point scale, 82% of 119 rated the conjunction higher, with means of 3.5 and 5.6. Replacing "bank teller" with "bank teller whether or not she is active in the feminist movement" left 57% of 75 still committing the fallacy, on mean ratings of 5.1 for the conjunction and 3.8 for the wider statement. Offered $10 to bet on one statement, 56% of 60 bet on the conjunction. The one manipulation that worked on Linda was expertise plus transparency: among 64 graduate students in the social sciences with credit for several statistics courses, 36% committed the fallacy. Wording mattered more in a problem built from classes rather than personality. Asked what percentage of surveyed men had had a heart attack and what percentage both were over 55 and had had one, 65% of 147 gave the second a higher figure. Adding a prior estimate of the percentage over 55 cut that to 31% of 159. Asking how many of 100 participants fell in each class cut it to 25% of 117, and adding the prior estimate as well cut it to 11% of 360.

replication.headline: Linda holds under real-money bets on unresolved future events and in a representative survey, frequency wording has cut it to near zero in some studies and left it standing in others, and the famous 85% is one sample's figure.
replication.detail: Chandrashekar, Cheng, Fong, Leung, Wong, Cheng and Feldman ran a preregistered replication of the adversarial collaboration on 1,032 MTurk participants, in four between-subject conditions with no filler items. Four responses met the preregistered exclusion rule and the report keeps the full sample. On Linda, estimates for "bank tellers and feminists" (M = 18.80) and "bank tellers and are feminists" (M = 19.55) both exceeded estimates for "bank tellers" (M = 9.87), with ds of 0.49, 95% CI [0.31, 0.67], and 0.50, 95% CI [0.32, 0.67]. On the James profile both conjunctions came out below the unlikely item alone, 15.19 and 15.55 against 18.38, and neither gap reached significance, so that half failed. Sides, Osherson, Bonini and Viale removed the two standard escape routes at once, using bets rather than probability judgments and sentences about verifiable future events rather than noun phrases. At Rice, 38 of 45 participants in the probability condition and 36 of 45 in the betting condition committed at least one of nine possible errors, with means of 3.4 and 3.2. At the University of Houston the figures were 29 of 29 and 25 of 28, means 5.93 and 4.86, and at Milan 90 of 92 and 60 of 60, means 4.33 and 4.85. Across the three experiments only 9% of betting participants avoided the fallacy altogether. A fourth experiment paid 50 cents a question and told participants that an independent judge would see only the sentence they left legible, which rules out reading "bank teller" as "bank teller and not a feminist": 28 of 43 in the explicit condition and 25 of 40 in the implicit condition still committed it. Toubia and colleagues put the between-subjects version to a US panel of 2,058 people recruited on Prolific by age, sex and ethnicity, each of whom saw one of the two statements. Linda was rated 2.43 as a bank teller and 3.38 as a feminist bank teller on a six-point scale at the first administration (t = -18.83, p < .001), and 2.52 against 3.35 at the second (t = -17.82, p < .001). What varies is the size. Charness, Karni and Levin gave the two-alternative version to 361 UCSB students and got 50 of 86 individuals wrong without incentives, 58.1%, against the 85.2% they were trying to reproduce. Paying $4 for the right answer brought it to 31 of 94, or 33.0%. Letting participants confer in pairs gave 48.2% and 13.2%, and in trios 25.6% and 10.4%. Marshall and Meins gave the Linda and Bill descriptions to 130 psychology undergraduates who rated each component and the conjunction from 0 to 100. With the description in front of them, 45% committed the fallacy on Linda and 40% on Bill; with only a name to go on, 19% did so on each. Yechiam and Zeif's meta-analysis of incentivisation, at n = 3,276, found d = 0.19 and an odds ratio of 1.40 for a correct answer when paid, with no moderating effect of payoff size, and reports that most of the studies it pools found no significant effect on their own.

study.cite: Chandrashekar, S. P., Cheng, Y. H., Fong, C. L., Leung, Y. C., Wong, Y. T., Cheng, B. L., & Feldman, G. (2021). Frequency estimation and semantic ambiguity do not eliminate conjunction bias, when it occurs: Replication and extension of Mellers, Hertwig, and Kahneman (2001). Meta-Psychology, 5.

limits: No multi-site or multi-laboratory replication was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and arXiv, and of the Many Labs and Registered Replication Report catalogues, turned up nothing, so the record is a set of single-laboratory studies, one preregistered online replication and one large online panel. That panel study, Toubia and colleagues, is a preprint, and its conjunction item is one task among about 28 in a 500-question dataset built for another purpose. Three of the effect's boundaries are well marked. The first is format. Hertwig and Gigerenzer found 0 of 20 and 3 of 23 participants violating the rule when the Linda problem asked how many of 200 women fell in each class, against 21 of 24 in a probability ranking, though their cells hold between 18 and 25 people. Gigerenzer's own summary of that literature puts the drop at about 85% to 20% and less. The second is content. Conjunction effects need a wide gap between the two constituents. In the 2021 replication, Linda drew estimates of 58.43 for feminists and 9.87 for bank tellers, while James drew 36.20 for artists and 18.38 for Republicans, and only Linda produced the effect. Mellers, Hertwig and Kahneman had already seen the James profile produce no conjunction effect at all in their first experiment, though it produced one with both "and" and "and are" in their third. The third is age. Marshall and Meins gave a social version of the task to 4- and 5-year-olds in two studies of 58 and 71 children and found errors at chance in both, while in a third study, of 148 children and 130 adults, 7- to 9-year-olds erred above chance. Error rates were unrelated to verbal ability, theory of mind and inhibitory control in the first two studies, and to prejudice and hindsight bias in the third. Fiedler's 1988 experiments still could not be opened. Springer's page for them redirects to an authentication endpoint, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy in any repository. The figures attributed to them here, 73% violations under probability wording against 23% under frequency wording in his first experiment and 70% against 25% in his second, are averages across the seven and five problems he ran, and are quoted from Hertwig and Gigerenzer's description, which puts his Linda frequency figure at 22% and then 17%.
misreadings: The 85% is treated as a property of the human mind rather than of one sample. It comes from a single two-alternative test on 142 UBC undergraduates. Charness, Karni and Levin ran that same version at UCSB and got 58%, a gap they tested and reported as reliable. Marshall and Meins, using rating scales on the same description, got 45% from 130 undergraduates. Sides and colleagues found more fallacies at the University of Houston than at Rice on almost the same items (F = 27.6, p < .001). Hertwig and Gigerenzer cite Hertwig and Chase's review of 17 conditions in 10 studies as finding a median of 87%, but that is for the ranking version of Linda, not the two-statement one, and the figure is quoted here from their description rather than from the review. The second error is treating the frequency format as a later refutation. Tversky and Kahneman reported it themselves in 1983, taking the health-survey problem from 65% to 25% by asking for counts out of 100, and Gigerenzer's case is about what that reduction means rather than about whether it happens. The third is assuming the word "and" is doing the damage. Mellers, Hertwig and Kahneman built an adversarial collaboration to settle it, agreeing the tests in advance with Mellers as arbiter. The unambiguous phrase "and are" behaved no differently from "and" in their first and third experiments, which Kahneman read as conclusive; in the second, with no filler items, the effect vanished for "and are" and survived for "and", which Hertwig read as support. The 2021 replication of that second experiment found no gap between the two phrasings, with a Bayes factor of 13.32 favouring the null on Linda, and Sides and colleagues found no gap between conjunctions marked by "and" and conjunctions marked by other constructions. The heuristic the effect was coined to demonstrate has its own entry here, under representativeness heuristic, as do base rate fallacy, extension neglect and subadditivity effect. What remains contested is the interpretation. Whether the fallacy shows a resemblance heuristic overriding logic, or a reasonable pragmatic reading of an ambiguous question, is a live argument. Whether people commit it is not.
